woodturning — Woodturning uses a lathe and hand-held tools to cut wood into forms symmetrical around the axis of rotation.
topiary — Topiary trains perennial plants into defined geometric or fanciful shapes by clipping their foliage and twigs.
an armature — A sculptor builds clay, wax, or another soft material around an armature for support and stability.
lost-wax casting — Lost-wax casting replaces a wax model with molten metal inside a heat-resistant mould.
a garden gnome — A garden gnome is a small humanoid lawn ornament commonly shown with a beard and pointed hat.
a mannequin — Shops use mannequins as human-shaped models for displaying clothing.
a Lego minifigure — A Lego minifigure is a small articulated plastic figurine designed for Lego construction sets.
a wax figure — A wax figure is a lifelike wax sculpture of a person, often displayed in a wax museum.
an action figure — Hasbro coined the term action figure in 1964 to market its poseable G.I. Joe character to boys while competitors called similar toys dolls.
a sand sculpture — Sand sculpture uses compacted sand and water to build forms that may be carved in detail.
a snow sculpture — Snow sculptures are shaped from compacted snow and are common features of winter festivals.
an ice sculpture — Ice sculptors carve blocks of ice with hand tools, power tools, or chainsaws.
balloon modelling — Balloon modelling shapes special balloons by twisting them into figures and decorations.
a butter sculpture — A butter sculpture is a three-dimensional artwork made from chilled butter.
a photo album — A photo album collects photographic prints in book form, often in sleeves or on heavy paper pages.
a contact print — A contact print is made with film held directly against photographic paper; a whole strip can form a contact sheet for selecting images.
a photographic enlarger — A photographic enlarger is a specialised projector used to produce prints from negatives or transparencies.
a camera obscura — A camera obscura forms an inverted projection when light enters a dark enclosure through a small opening.
a tintype — A tintype is a direct positive photograph made on a thin sheet of iron coated with dark lacquer or enamel.
a photo booth — A photo booth contains an automated camera and processor that produces portraits, often in a strip.
a disposable camera — A disposable camera is sold with film inside and is usually handed in whole for processing.
an instant camera — An instant camera uses self-developing film to produce a physical photograph soon after exposure.
a slide projector — A slide projector shines light through a photographic slide and projects an enlarged image onto a screen.
a stereoscope — A stereoscope presents a slightly different photograph to each eye, creating an impression of depth.
a diorama — A diorama is a three-dimensional replica of a scene; museum habitat dioramas often combine models with a painted background.
a travelling exhibition — A travelling exhibition is designed to be presented at several venues instead of staying in one place.
an audio guide — An audio guide provides recorded spoken commentary for visitors to a museum or other attraction.
an exhibition catalogue — An exhibition catalogue records the works presented in an art exhibition and often adds descriptions or essays.
a permanent collection — A museum's permanent collection consists of assets it owns, whether or not they are currently on display.
a thatched roof — A thatched roof is built from layered dry vegetation, commonly straw, reeds, rushes, or similar plants.
a spiral staircase — A spiral staircase winds around a central post or open space while gaining height.
a chimney pot — A chimney pot extends the flue above the chimney stack and can help improve the draught.
a French balcony — A French or Juliet balcony is a balconet: a railing across a full-height opening with little or no projecting platform.
a curtain wall — A curtain wall is a non-structural exterior wall attached to a building's load-bearing frame.
a paper fortune teller — A paper fortune teller is a folded paper toy operated with the fingers to reveal hidden messages.
a paper plane — A paper plane is a toy aircraft, usually a glider, made from a single folded sheet of paper or paperboard.
papier-mâché — Papier-mâché combines paper pieces or pulp with an adhesive so it can dry into a shaped object.
decoupage — Decoupage decorates an object with glued paper cut-outs and commonly finishes it with protective varnish.
paper marbling — Paper marbling floats colours on water or another liquid surface and transfers the resulting stone-like pattern to paper.
a children's museum — Children's museums design exhibitions and activities around children's learning and participation.
a natural history museum — Natural history museums preserve collections covering living things, fossils, geology and other parts of nature.
a museum ship — A museum ship is a preserved former vessel that has been converted into a museum open to the public.
a virtual museum — A virtual museum presents a digitally recorded collection through electronic media, commonly online.
an archaeological museum — Archaeological museums specialise in archaeological artifacts; some, including the Ancient Agora and Roman Forum, are open-air.
a handrail — A handrail is designed to be grasped by the hand for support, especially on stairs.
a revolving door — A revolving door has several leaves attached to a central shaft and rotates within a round enclosure.
a mezzanine — A mezzanine is an intermediate floor that does not cover the entire space and may overlook the floor below.
a lightwell — A lightwell is an open vertical space designed to bring light and ventilation into interior rooms.
a dumbwaiter — A dumbwaiter is a small freight lift used to move objects rather than people between floors.
an igloo — An igloo is a shelter built from suitable snow and traditionally used in parts of the Arctic.
a houseboat — A houseboat is a boat designed or modified primarily for regular dwelling.
a shipping-container home — Shipping-container architecture adapts intermodal freight containers into homes and other buildings.
a yurt — A yurt is a portable round dwelling traditionally covered and insulated with felt or skins.
a stilt house — Stilt houses are raised above land or water and are often built to reduce flood risk.
a car wash — A car wash is a facility designed to clean the outside and sometimes the inside of motor vehicles.
a fire station — A fire station houses firefighting vehicles, equipment and working areas for firefighters.
a hangar — A hangar is built to store and protect aircraft and to support maintenance and repair work.
a boathouse — A boathouse is a building beside or over water that shelters boats.
a signal box — A signal box contains equipment used to control railway points and signals.
Pop art — Pop art borrowed imagery from mass culture, including advertising, comics, celebrities and everyday products.
Cubism — Cubism broke subjects apart and reassembled them in abstract forms, often combining multiple viewpoints.
Futurism — Futurism emphasized speed, technology and modern machines such as cars and aeroplanes.
kinetic art — Kinetic art incorporates real or apparent movement, including works driven by motors, wind or water.
Constructivism — Constructivism began in Russia and connected abstract geometric design with modern materials and social aims.
land art — Land art uses landscapes and materials found in nature, including earth, rock, plants and water.
sound art — Sound art uses sound as its primary time-based medium or material.
body art — Body art is made on, with or through the human body, which becomes part of the artwork.
video art — Video art uses video as a visual or audiovisual medium and often works outside conventional cinema storytelling.
conceptual art — Conceptual art gives the concept or idea equal or greater importance than traditional visual and technical concerns.
a coloured pencil — A coloured pencil has a narrow pigmented core enclosed in a wooden case.
a crayon — A crayon is a stick of pigmented wax used for writing or drawing.
a gel pen — A gel pen suspends pigment in a water-based gel; its thick, opaque ink comes in bright, metallic and glittery colours.
a mechanical pencil — A mechanical pencil pushes a replaceable solid marking core through its tip and does not need ordinary sharpening.
an oil pastel — Oil pastels bind pigment with non-drying oil and wax, producing a soft, greasy drawing medium.
cross-stitch — Cross-stitch is a form of counted-thread embroidery in which X-shaped stitches form a tiled picture or pattern.
crochet — Crochet interlocks loops of yarn or thread with a crochet hook.
lace making — Lace is an open patterned fabric made by looping, twisting or braiding threads.
felting — Felting turns fibres into felt by matting, condensing and pressing them together.
appliqué — Appliqué is ornamental needlework in which shaped fabric pieces are sewn or stuck onto a larger piece to form a picture or pattern.
plywood — Plywood is made by stacking and gluing thin wood veneers, usually with the grain of adjacent layers running at right angles.
drywall — Drywall is a gypsum panel faced with heavy paper and used to construct interior walls and ceilings.
flat glass — Flat glass is manufactured in a plane form and is widely used in windows, doors and glazed walls.
rammed earth — Rammed-earth construction compresses a damp soil mixture in layers inside formwork to create solid walls.
cross-laminated timber — Cross-laminated timber glues solid-wood boards in perpendicular layers to form strong structural panels.
sandpaper — Sandpaper is paper or cloth coated with abrasive grit and is commonly used to smooth surfaces.
polishing — Polishing creates a smooth, shiny surface through rubbing or chemical treatment.
gilding — Gilding applies a thin coating of gold to surfaces such as metal, wood, porcelain or stone.
shellac — Shellac is a natural resin commonly dissolved in alcohol and used as a glossy wood finish.
gesso — Gesso is a white primer mixture used to prepare canvas, wooden panels and other surfaces for paint.
Roy Lichtenstein — Drowning Girl uses a simplified comic-strip style and hand-painted dots that imitate commercial printing.
Vincent van Gogh — Van Gogh used clashing red and green in The Night Café to make the all-night room feel oppressive rather than welcoming.
Johannes Vermeer — Vermeer’s The Milkmaid turns an ordinary domestic task into a carefully lit study of stillness and concentration.
Henri Matisse — Matisse reduced Dance to five linked bodies and three intense fields of colour, making rhythm more important than realistic detail.
Edward Hopper — Hopper’s Automat uses the bright interior and unreadable night window to intensify the sitter’s urban isolation.
The Son of Man — Magritte’s The Son of Man frustrates portrait recognition by hiding most of the face behind an ordinary apple.
The Garden of Earthly Delights — The Garden of Earthly Delights contrasts paradise, a fantastical central world and punishment across its three panels.

assertion: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère — Manet’s last major painting sets the barmaid against a mirror whose puzzling reflections include the crowd and a customer.

supportingSource.title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère — Wikipedia

assertion: The Sleeping Gypsy — The Sleeping Gypsy combines a reclining traveller, a watchful lion and a moonlit desert in Rousseau’s deliberately dreamlike style.
The Raft of the Medusa — The Raft of the Medusa turns a notorious shipwreck into a rising pyramid of exhausted bodies balanced between despair and possible rescue.

supportingSource.title: The Raft of the Medusa — Wikipedia

assertion: Pietà — Michelangelo carved the Pietà as a compact pyramid of two figures, balancing grief with an unusually calm Virgin Mary.
Winged Victory of Samothrace — The Winged Victory was designed for a ship-shaped base, so its wind-blown drapery makes the stone figure appear to land at sea.
Cloud Gate — Anish Kapoor’s Cloud Gate is made from joined steel plates polished so smoothly that its seams disappear.
Maman — Bourgeois linked the giant spider Maman to her own mother, combining a protective egg sac with a form that can also feel threatening.
The Burghers of Calais — The Burghers of Calais commemorates citizens who offered themselves to Edward III during the Hundred Years’ War to save their city.
Zaha Hadid — Zaha Hadid Architects designed the centre so that its plaza, walls and roof flow into one another with few visible corners.
Oscar Niemeyer — Niemeyer designed the cathedral’s hyperboloid structure from sixteen concrete columns, making the roof appear open to the sky.
Norman Foster — Foster’s firm designed the tower with a spiralling structural grid and air shafts that reduce the need for conventional air conditioning.
Tadao Ando — Ando’s chapel uses bare concrete and the luminous cross to turn changing daylight into its principal decoration.
Daniel Libeskind — Libeskind made disorientation and absence part of the museum’s architecture through sloping routes, sharp angles and inaccessible voids.
the Chrysler Building — The Chrysler Building’s terraced metal crown and spire made it one of the clearest symbols of the skyscraper age.
the Palace of Westminster — The Palace of Westminster was rebuilt in the Gothic Revival style after a fire, with the Commons and Lords meeting inside.
the Lotus Temple — The Lotus Temple is a Baháʼí house of worship whose petal-like shells form nine sides around a central hall.
Hundertwasserhaus — Hundertwasserhaus follows Friedensreich Hundertwasser’s belief that residents, irregular forms and vegetation should enliven mass housing.
CopenHill — CopenHill, also called Amager Bakke, combines an industrial power plant with an artificial ski slope and public recreation on its roof.
Minimalism — Minimalism emphasized the object itself and the viewer’s experience; minimalist painting often used hard edges, straight lines and simple forms.

assertion: Neoclassicism — Neoclassicism drew on archaeological interest in antiquity and favoured clear outlines, order and moral seriousness.
Expressionism — Expressionism values the artist’s subjective emotional response, often using exaggeration and intense colour.
Brutalism — Brutalist buildings make structure and materials explicit, especially rough concrete known as béton brut.
Op art — Op art uses precise abstract patterns to create optical effects such as vibration, swelling or apparent motion.
fresco — In true fresco, pigment becomes part of the wall surface as the lime plaster sets, which is why the method suits murals.
impasto — The Italian-derived term describes paint thick enough to stand out from the canvas; oil and heavy-body acrylic are common media.
pointillism — Pointillism relies on optical mixing: adjacent dots remain distinct on the canvas but combine in perception.
chiaroscuro — Chiaroscuro uses graded or sharp light-dark contrast to make painted figures and spaces appear three-dimensional.
trompe-l’œil — Trompe-l’œil means “deceive the eye” and uses perspective, shadow and scale to simulate physical depth or objects.
the Museum of Modern Art — The Museum of Modern Art built a collection around modern painting, sculpture, design, photography and film.
the Art Institute of Chicago — The Art Institute of Chicago holds especially strong collections of American and Impressionist art as well as design and world art.
the Van Gogh Museum — The Van Gogh Museum preserves hundreds of the artist’s paintings and drawings together with his letters and works by contemporaries.
the Peggy Guggenheim Collection — The collection occupies Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, where Guggenheim lived and assembled a personal survey of modern art.
the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art — Louisiana was designed as a sequence of buildings and landscape, so visitors move repeatedly between art, gardens and views of the sound.

supportingSource.title: Louisiana Museum of Modern Art — Wikipedia

assertion: the Oslo Opera House — The Oslo Opera House extends its pale stone roof down to plaza level, making the building itself a public promenade.
Hallgrímskirkja — Hallgrímskirkja’s central tower and descending side wings echo the columnar basalt found in Icelandic landscapes.
Temppeliaukio Church — Temppeliaukio Church leaves the rough excavated rock visible inside beneath a disc-like copper roof.
Turning Torso — Santiago Calatrava based Turning Torso on a sculpture of a twisting human body, rotating the tower’s sections as they rise.
the Black Diamond — The Black Diamond’s polished dark façade reflects the harbour, while its central atrium opens the heavy exterior toward the water.
Georgia O’Keeffe — O’Keeffe repeatedly enlarged natural forms and drew on New Mexico landscapes and animal skulls, making them central to her distinctive modernism.
Marc Chagall — Chagall built a personal visual world from Vitebsk village life, Jewish tradition and figures that float through vividly coloured scenes.
David Hockney — After moving to Los Angeles, Hockney made swimming pools and bright acrylic colour recurring features of his California paintings.
Fernando Botero — Botero’s style, often called Boterismo, enlarges the volume of figures for effects that can range from humour to political criticism.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude — Christo and Jeanne-Claude transformed familiar places with temporary installations, including Wrapped Reichstag and The Gates in Central Park.
the Royal Albert Hall — The Royal Albert Hall opened as a vast oval auditorium and remains closely identified with the annual Proms concerts.
the Vienna State Opera — The Vienna State Opera was one of the first major public buildings completed on the Ringstrasse and is the setting of the Vienna Opera Ball.
Walt Disney Concert Hall — Walt Disney Concert Hall pairs Gehry’s sculptural metal exterior with a vineyard-style auditorium designed around the orchestra.
the Elbphilharmonie — The Elbphilharmonie reuses the Kaispeicher warehouse as a base for a glazed upper building with a rising and falling roofline.
Harpa — Harpa’s modular glass façade changes with daylight and reflections, turning the harbour building into a luminous geometric landmark.
the Burj Al Arab — The Burj Al Arab uses a curved outer frame and a translucent fibreglass façade to create the silhouette of a billowing sail.
Beijing National Stadium — Beijing National Stadium exposes its irregular steel lattice as both structure and image, creating the nest-like appearance behind its Bird’s Nest nickname.
the Cube Houses — Piet Blom tilted each cube onto a hexagonal pylon, raising dense housing while leaving useful public space at ground level.
the Crooked House — The Polish name Krzywy Domek means Crooked House, and its designers drew on illustrations by Jan Marcin Szancer and Per Dahlberg.
Kunsthaus Graz — Kunsthaus Graz combines blob architecture with an acrylic-glass façade that can display changing images like a giant low-resolution screen.
the Hollywood Sign — The Hollywood Sign began as an advertisement for a housing development and later lost its final four letters to become a film-industry symbol.
Uncle Sam — James Montgomery Flagg’s recruiting image adapted the national personification Uncle Sam into a direct appeal to each viewer.
Keep Calm and Carry On — The government prepared the Keep Calm and Carry On poster in 1939 for a severe wartime crisis, but it was barely displayed at the time.

supportingSource.title: Keep Calm and Carry On — Wikipedia

assertion: Kilroy was here — The phrase and doodle became associated with American servicemen during World War II, although their exact origin remains disputed.
the London Underground roundel — The London Underground roundel developed from an early solid red disc into the familiar open circle crossed by a blue name bar.
Garfield — Jim Davis built Garfield’s humour around appetite, laziness and sarcastic commentary on the people and pets around him.
Snoopy — Snoopy began as Charlie Brown’s dog but gained an elaborate fantasy life that turns the doghouse into aircraft and other settings.
Tintin — Tintin’s simple face, distinctive quiff and partnership with Snowy make him immediately recognisable across Hergé’s adventure series.
Asterix — Asterix pairs quick wits with temporary superhuman strength from Getafix’s potion while defending his village from Rome.
Wally — Wally is deliberately drawn with a strong striped pattern and repeated amid visual distractions, turning each spread into a search puzzle.
the Sibelius Monument — Eila Hiltunen arranged over 600 steel tubes to evoke Sibelius’s music and added the composer’s portrait after debate over the abstract design.

assertion: Fearless Girl — Fearless Girl was installed for International Women’s Day in 2017 and later moved to a position facing the New York Stock Exchange.
The Motherland Calls — The Motherland Calls forms the dramatic centre of the memorial to the Battle of Stalingrad and was once the world’s tallest statue.
the Angel of the North — Antony Gormley designed the Angel of the North with a 54-metre wingspan, marking a former coal-mining landscape in northeast England.
The Kelpies — The Kelpies honour the heavy horses that powered Scottish industry and waterways, translating their heads into vast steel structures.
Adidas — Adidas used three stripes on footwear before the simple repeated bands became a trademark across its clothing and equipment.
Mercedes-Benz — Mercedes-Benz inherited the three-pointed star from Daimler, where it expressed an ambition to motorise travel across land, water and air.
FedEx — FedEx’s 1994 wordmark uses tightly fitted letterforms so the negative space between its final letters forms an arrow suggesting speed and direction.
Lacoste — René Lacoste was nicknamed the Crocodile, and the animal became an unusually early example of a logo displayed on the outside of clothing.
Toblerone — Toblerone pairs its triangular bars with a mountain mark containing Bern’s heraldic animal, linking product shape and place of origin.
the University of Tartu main building — The main building was constructed from 1804 to 1809 for the reopened university and remains its architectural symbol.

supportingSource.title: Main building of Tartu University — Wikipedia

assertion: the Estonian National Museum — The Estonian National Museum’s new building incorporates the history of Raadi manor, war and the former military airfield into its design.
Tartu Cathedral — The former choir of Tartu Cathedral was converted for the university library, which moved there in 1806; it later became home to the university museum.

assertion: Haapsalu Railway Station — The station complex joins a 216-metre covered platform to a wooden-lace terminal and a two-storey stone waiting room with a clock tower.
Kreenholm Manufacture — Kreenholm developed around a nineteenth-century cotton mill whose island factories drew power from eleven water turbines.
the Swiss Army knife — The Swiss Army knife grew from a soldier’s pocket tool into a compact family of folding implements recognised by its red scales.
a lava lamp — Edward Craven Walker introduced the lava lamp in 1963; the bulb’s heat lowers the wax’s density so it rises, while cooling makes it sink again.
Vespa — The Vespa combined enclosed mechanical parts, a step-through frame and a distinctive pressed-steel body into a practical post-war scooter.
Zippo — Zippo has kept the same basic rectangular case, hinged top and protected wick for decades, making its sound and silhouette widely recognisable.
Chuck Taylor All-Stars — Converse developed the shoes for basketball, added Chuck Taylor’s signature to the ankle patch and kept the basic canvas-and-rubber design largely unchanged.
Buckingham Palace — Buckingham Palace became the monarch’s principal London residence and its east-front balcony provides a stage for national celebrations.
Topkapı Palace — Topkapı Palace served as the Ottoman court and administrative centre for centuries, organised as successive gates and courtyards rather than one single block.
Schönbrunn Palace — Schönbrunn Palace grew into the Habsburgs’ great summer residence, joining ceremonial interiors to extensive gardens and the Gloriette.
the Potala Palace — The Potala Palace combines the White Palace, used for government and residence, with the sacred Red Palace on Marpo Ri.
Pena Palace — King Ferdinand II transformed a ruined monastery into Pena Palace, combining historic styles in a theatrical hilltop composition.
Saint Basil’s Cathedral — Saint Basil’s Cathedral was built for Ivan IV and combines separate chapels around a central church into its famous cluster of domes.
the Western Wall — The Western Wall is part of the ancient retaining system around the Temple Mount and is Judaism’s most prominent public prayer site.
the Blue Mosque — The Blue Mosque takes its popular name from the blue-toned İznik tiles that decorate the interior of Sultan Ahmed I’s mosque.
Chartres Cathedral — Chartres Cathedral preserves an exceptional ensemble of medieval stained glass, while its mismatched spires record different building periods.
the Shwedagon Pagoda — The Shwedagon Pagoda is Myanmar’s most sacred Buddhist site, centred on a gold-covered stupa whose form is visible across Yangon.
the Brooklyn Bridge — The Brooklyn Bridge joined Manhattan and Brooklyn with a hybrid cable-stayed suspension design and a raised pedestrian promenade.
the Ponte Vecchio — The Ponte Vecchio combines three stone arches with shop-lined passageways and the later corridor linking the Medici palaces.
the Forth Bridge — The Forth Bridge’s exposed steel cantilevers made its structure visually legible and turned it into an icon of late Victorian engineering.
the Millau Viaduct — The Millau Viaduct carries the A75 across the Tarn valley, with exceptionally tall piers supporting a light cable-stayed deck.
the Helix Bridge — The Helix Bridge links Marina Centre and Marina South, using paired spirals and viewing pods to frame the bay.
the CN Tower — The CN Tower was built for telecommunications and became Toronto’s defining observation landmark after opening in 1976.
the Berlin TV Tower — The Berlin TV Tower became a socialist-era skyline symbol, while the sunlit cross on its sphere acquired the nickname “Pope’s Revenge”.
Tokyo Skytree — Tokyo Skytree opened as the broadcasting centre for the capital region, with its 634-metre height chosen partly for the Musashi wordplay.
the Oriental Pearl Tower — The Oriental Pearl Tower uses a sequence of large and small spheres to create one of Pudong’s most recognisable silhouettes.
KL Tower — KL Tower is a telecommunications and observation structure set within one of Kuala Lumpur’s oldest forest reserves.
the Gardens of Versailles — André Le Nôtre’s vast formal plan turned the landscape west of the palace into a model copied by royal gardens across Europe.
Keukenhof — Dutch bulb growers use Keukenhof as a seasonal showcase, replanting its flower beds with new designs each year.
Gardens by the Bay — Its Supertrees are vertical gardens that also collect solar energy and rainwater, joining spectacle with environmental systems.
Ryōan-ji — From any normal viewing position, at least one of the fifteen rocks remains hidden, making the spare composition change with the viewer.
the Butchart Gardens — Jennie Butchart began transforming the worked-out quarry, and the estate later added Japanese, Italian and rose gardens.
Ansel Adams — Adams paired large-format landscape photography with the Zone System, a method for controlling tones from deep shadow to bright snow.
Dorothea Lange — Lange’s documentary work gave individual faces to poverty and migration, influencing both public opinion and later photojournalism.
Robert Capa — Capa said that he exposed 106 frames on Omaha Beach, but only eleven survived; the familiar story that the rest were ruined in a London darkroom has since been disputed.
Henri Cartier-Bresson — Cartier-Bresson sought the instant when gesture and geometry briefly align, and he was another founding member of Magnum Photos.
Man Ray — The technique existed before him as the photogram, but Man Ray’s playful objects and shadows made his personal name for it famous.
the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao — The building’s international success gave rise to the “Bilbao effect”, the idea that daring cultural architecture can help remake a city’s image.
the Louvre Abu Dhabi — Jean Nouvel layered the dome’s geometric lattice so moving spots of sunlight recall rays filtering through palm leaves.
the Museum of the Future — The calligraphic windows reproduce quotations about the future by Dubai’s ruler, turning written lines into part of the structure.
the Niterói Contemporary Art Museum — Its viewing gallery frames Guanabara Bay, Rio de Janeiro and Sugarloaf Mountain, making the landscape part of the museum visit.
the National Museum of Qatar — The discs create sheltered cavities against the desert heat, while an older palace remains at the heart of the museum site.
bone china — Bone china is one of the strongest white ceramics; bone ash helps produce its characteristic whiteness and translucency.
Delftware — Delft potters adapted the look of imported Asian porcelain to local earthenware, producing tiles as well as vessels.
Murano glass — Venice moved its glass furnaces to Murano in the Middle Ages, concentrating skilled workshops and reducing fire risk in the city.
raku ware — Raku developed in connection with the tea ceremony, where each bowl’s irregular form and glaze effects are appreciated individually.
Jasperware — Josiah Wedgwood developed the stoneware in the 1770s, and its cameo-like reliefs suited the era’s taste for antiquity.
tartan — Although particular patterns became associated with clans, tartan is also used by institutions, regions and fashion designers.
an Indian sari — Regional styles differ in how the cloth is pleated and draped, while a fitted blouse and underskirt commonly support it.
an Aran jumper — It takes its name from a group of islands off Ireland’s west coast and became an international image of Irish craft during the twentieth century.
kente cloth — Colours and motifs can carry named meanings, and cloth once linked to royalty is now worn at major celebrations.
ikat — Because the design is planned in the yarns, the weaver must align dyed sections as the cloth gradually takes shape.
sepia — The word links the reddish-brown ink once derived from cuttlefish with a photographic toning process that turns black-and-white prints brown.
ultramarine — Painters often reserved the costly natural pigment for the Virgin Mary’s robes, while a synthetic version later made the colour widely affordable.
Prussian blue — In cyanotype printing, light acts on photosensitive iron salts to form an insoluble Prussian blue image; the pigment is the result of the process.

Whistler’s Mother — James McNeill Whistler titled the work Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, but the sitter was his mother and the popular nickname endured.
Lady with an Ermine — The sitter is generally identified as Cecilia Gallerani, and the ermine may allude both to purity and to her patron Ludovico Sforza.

The Laughing Cavalier — The unknown sitter is not actually laughing, and the romantic title was added centuries after Hals painted him.
the Rubin vase — Perception alternates between figure and background, so the viewer cannot normally see both interpretations as the foreground at once.
the Penrose stairs — Lionel and Roger Penrose popularised the continuous loop, and M. C. Escher later made a famous version in Ascending and Descending.
the Ames room — Its irregular walls place one corner farther from the viewer, while a fixed peephole makes the space look like an ordinary rectangular room.
the café wall illusion — Alternating contrast along the offset tile edges shifts the apparent position of each line even though a ruler shows them parallel.
the impossible trident — The lines supply locally plausible edges that cannot belong to one consistent three-dimensional object when followed across the whole drawing.
Liberty Leading the People — Delacroix combined a real street uprising with Liberty as an allegorical figure striding over the fallen.
The Third of May 1808 — The victim’s raised arms echo a crucifixion pose, while the soldiers turn their faces away and become a mechanical wall of rifles.
Flower Thrower — The work is also known as Love Is in the Air, a title that sharpens its contrast between violent posture and peaceful object.
The Problem We All Live With — Rockwell omitted the marshals’ heads and focused the viewer on the small child, a tomato stain and a racial slur on the wall.

assertion: Do Women Have to Be Naked to Get into the Met. Museum? — The anonymous collective used humour, advertising graphics and hard numbers to expose the gap between female nudes on display and women represented as artists.
the Buddhas of Bamiyan — The two sixth-century reliefs stood 38 and 55 metres high; their bodies were hewn from the cliff and finished with mud-and-straw modelling and stucco.
Ad Deir — The Nabataean building probably served a religious or commemorative role and may later have been repurposed as a church in the Byzantine period.
Sigiriya — King Kashyapa built a palace on the summit and gardens below; the surviving paws mark the entrance once shaped as a huge lion.
the Ellora Caves — Kailasa was cut downward from a single mass of basalt, removing rock to reveal a freestanding temple rather than assembling one block by block.
the Longmen Grottoes — Work continued under several dynasties, producing niches that range from tiny images to the monumental Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple.
Casa Azul — Kahlo lived there for much of her life with family and later Diego Rivera; rooms preserve paintings, folk art and personal objects.
the Dalí Theatre-Museum — The old auditorium became an open-air courtyard, making the surviving theatre spaces part of the Surrealist spectacle.
the Rembrandt House Museum — The inventory helped restorers recover the arrangement of the rooms, art collection and working spaces seen by visitors.
the Pollock-Krasner House and Studio — One artist began using the barn in 1946; after his death, his widow used the same building as her workplace.
Carl Larsson-gården — The Arts and Crafts-influenced rooms offered a striking alternative to the era’s heavy bourgeois interiors.
Marilyn Diptych — Warhol made the paired panels soon after Marilyn Monroe’s death, contrasting a bright celebrity image with increasingly faint impressions.
My Bed — Emin based the installation on a depressive period when she remained in bed for four days; it was later exhibited at Tate.
Rabbit — Koons incorporated the inflatable rabbit as a readymade object and transformed it into a highly polished stainless-steel piece.
Love is in the Bin — The work had been known as Girl with Balloon; Pest Control renamed it Love is in the Bin.

Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe — The contemporary scene was rejected by the Salon jury of 1863 and exhibited at the Salon des Refusés, where it sparked notoriety and controversy.
Tilted Arc — The site-specific sculpture bisected the plaza; it was removed in 1989 after a public hearing and litigation, despite Serra’s argument that relocation would destroy the work.
Bird in Space — The 1928 judges found for the artist; this became the first court decision to accept non-representational sculpture as art.
The Gross Clinic — Its unsparing surgery scene was considered unsuitable for the art gallery and shown instead in the exhibition’s medical section.
Equivalent VIII — The Tate purchase drew press criticism over taxpayers’ money; the work consists of 120 firebricks arranged in two layers as a six-by-ten rectangle.
London Bridge — Numbered granite facing blocks from the nineteenth-century bridge were attached to a new concrete structure in Arizona.
Dresden Frauenkirche — Rebuilders reused about 3,800 surviving stones; their darker patina makes the old material visibly different from the new.
Stari Most — The bridge crosses the Neretva and connects two parts of Mostar; after reconstruction it reopened on 23 July 2004.
the Temple of Debod — Egypt donated the sanctuary in gratitude for Spain’s help in the international rescue effort prompted by the Aswan High Dam.

the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour — The palace project stalled and was never completed; reconstruction of the cathedral began in 1994 after an architect had initially been asked to design a replica.

assertion: The Slav Epic — Mucha worked on the cycle for eighteen years and gave it to Prague on condition that the city build a special pavilion for it.
the Black Paintings — Goya probably never intended the wall images for public exhibition; they were later attached to canvas, and the Black Paintings are now in Madrid’s Museo del Prado.
the Seagram Murals — Rothko made three sets totalling about forty mural-sized canvases and donated nine to London’s Tate Gallery in 1969.
The Migration Series — Lawrence planned the captions and images together, treating the historic mass movement as one continuous visual narrative.
The Course of Empire — Some critics read the boulder visible throughout the series as contrasting the earth’s immutability with human transience.
the Eames House — Charles and Ray Eames changed the scheme to avoid the meadow and preserved an existing row of eucalyptus trees.
the Farnsworth House — The house is cited as a major International Style work; Mies chose steel and glass and raised it above the Fox River floodplain.
the Rietveld Schröder House — Sliding and revolving panels let its upper living level remain open or be divided into three bedrooms, a bathroom and a living room.
Villa Mairea — Designed for Maire and Harry Gullichsen, the villa’s dining-room axis looks through clerestory windows into the pine forest.
E-1027 — Gray also designed furniture for the house, including an adjustable tubular-steel table made for eating in bed.
The Treachery of Images — The text says that the image is not an actual pipe, turning the gap between an object, its picture and the words for it into the work’s subject.
The Ambassadors — The skull is intended as a vanitas or memento mori, and its anamorphosis requires the viewer to approach from high right or low left.

The Human Condition — At first, viewers may assume that the canvas depicts the portion of landscape outside the window that it hides from view, making them question whether they see outdoors or its representation.
Triple Self-Portrait — Small reproductions of self-portraits by Dürer, Rembrandt, Picasso and van Gogh are pinned beside Rockwell’s easel.
The Art of Painting — Her laurel wreath and trumpet, and a possible history book, support the Clio reading, although Fama and Pictura are also proposed.
the ampersand — Its English name is a corruption of “and per se and”, meaning “& by itself = and”.
the euro sign — The European Commission presented the winning design after reducing thirty proposals to a public-survey shortlist.
the biohazard symbol — The designers tested candidate shapes for recognition and recall, then paired the selected mark with one fixed warning association.
the Command key symbol — Kare found the looped-square form in a symbol dictionary; Nordic countries used it for cultural locations and places of interest.
the Woolmark — A 1963 competition selected the logo credited to Francesco Saroglia, probably a pseudonym used by designer Franco Grignani.
the Amber Room — The room was constructed in eighteenth-century Prussia and later disappeared during World War II; its fate and current whereabouts, if it survived, remain a mystery.
the Rothko Chapel — The chapel serves as a place of meditation, and its skylight diffuser distributes light evenly onto the paintings.
The Red Studio — Matisse covered a pale-yellow ground with thin red paint, leaving the earlier layer visible as outlines around furniture.
the Peacock Room — The artist altered the room far beyond the owner’s request, and their quarrel became part of the history encoded in the battling birds.
the Merzbau — The Hanover original was destroyed in an Allied bombing raid in 1943; Hanover’s Sprengel Museum has a reconstruction of its first room.
the Jet d’Eau — The hydraulic safety-valve jet’s aesthetic value was recognized, and it was moved for the 1891 celebrations; it was later enlarged.
the Dubai Fountain — WET Design, also responsible for the Bellagio fountains, designed the system; its performances combine light and music.

the Fountain of the Four Rivers — The river gods represent the Nile for Africa, Danube for Europe, Ganges for Asia and Río de la Plata for the Americas; travertine rocks support them beneath the obelisk and Pamphili emblem.
Crown Fountain — The changing portraits depict Chicago residents and update the old fountain tradition of water emerging from sculpted faces.
the Stravinsky Fountain — Jean Tinguely’s black mechanisms and Niki de Saint Phalle’s bright figures animate the pool in contrasting styles.

the Venus of Willendorf — Its non-local limestone and red ochre give researchers evidence for studying the movement of Ice Age people and raw materials without proving where the finished figure was carved.
the Nefertiti Bust — The bust became a world-renowned icon of Nefertiti and is displayed at Berlin’s Neues Museum.
Laocoön and His Sons — The group has been called a prototypical icon of human agony; its contorted expressions are mirrored in struggling, straining bodies.
the Dying Gaul — The Roman marble is thought to copy a lost Hellenistic bronze made to commemorate victory over the Galatians while portraying the defeated warrior with dignity.
the Standard of Ur — Its shell, red limestone and lapis-lazuli mosaics are conventionally called the War and Peace panels, though the object’s original function is uncertain.
the Church of Saint George, Lalibela — The church was excavated downward from volcanic tuff; both its roof and its plan form a Greek cross.

supportingSource.title: Church of Saint George, Lalibela — Wikipedia

assertion: Great Zimbabwe — It served as the capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe; Rhodesia’s white government later pressured archaeologists to deny that black Africans had built it.
the Hassan II Mosque — The mosque stands partly over the Atlantic on a platform built from a natural rock outcrop, and its laser-topped minaret points toward Mecca.
the pyramids of Meroë — In the 1830s Giuseppe Ferlini sought treasure at Meroë and demolished several pyramids; Nubian pyramids are closely arranged in clusters.
Fasil Ghebbi — Emperors Yohannes I, Iyasu I and Dawit III added structures to the imperial compound, considerably expanding the enclosure.
Diego Rivera — Rivera’s large frescoes helped establish Mexican muralism; his public commissions extended from Mexico City to Detroit and New York.
Tarsila do Amaral — Tarsila’s 1928 painting inspired Oswald de Andrade’s Anthropophagite Manifesto and became an emblem of a distinctly Brazilian modernism.
Joaquín Torres-García — The inverted continent made South America its own visual “north” and expressed Torres-García’s call for regional cultural independence.
Wifredo Lam — Lam fused European avant-garde approaches with Afro-Cuban culture rather than presenting that culture as picturesque folklore.
Remedios Varo — Varo reached Mexico City as a wartime exile in 1941; her mature work there turned scientific and occult ideas into meticulous Surrealist scenes.
Sonia Delaunay — Delaunay treated colour and rhythm as a shared language across abstract painting, printed fabric, clothing and commercial design.
Hilma af Klint — Af Klint’s abstract work predates several celebrated pioneers of abstraction and gives complex spiritual concepts a visual form.
Hannah Höch — Höch was one of the originators of photomontage, turning mass-produced press images into disruptive new compositions.
Barbara Hepworth — In 1931 Hepworth began making the pierced forms that became characteristic of her sculpture and later influenced Henry Moore.
Lee Krasner — Krasner repeatedly reworked her own art; collage became one of several forms alongside her gestural paintings and Little Image series.
Tate Modern — The museum opened in the converted power station in 2000; the central Turbine Hall preserves the scale of the industrial building.
the High Line — The linear park reuses the southern part of the former New York Central Railroad West Side Line as a public greenway.
Battersea Power Station — Two matching station halves produced its famous four-chimney silhouette; later redevelopment retained the landmark shell for public and commercial uses.
Zeitz MOCAA — Heatherwick Studio converted the historic grain silo into a museum for contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora.

supportingSource.title: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa — Wikipedia

assertion: the Vienna Gasometers — The protected nineteenth-century exteriors now surround new interiors divided among living, working, shopping and cultural uses.
the National September 11 Memorial — Michael Arad and Peter Walker’s design uses the towers’ empty footprints as pools and arranges the inscribed names by meaningful relationships.
Shoes on the Danube Bank — Victims were ordered to remove their valuable shoes before being shot into the Danube; the sculpture represents what they left behind.

supportingSource.title: Shoes on the Danube Bank — Wikipedia

assertion: the AIDS Memorial Quilt — Cleve Jones conceived the quilt after a march whose placards of names resembled a patchwork when taped to a building.

supportingSource.title: NAMES Project AIDS Memorial Quilt — Wikipedia

assertion: the Sarajevo Roses — Shell bursts left floral fragmentation patterns in the pavement; colouring selected scars red turned damage into memorial “roses”.
the National Memorial for Peace and Justice — The hanging monuments represent United States counties with documented lynchings; matching copies were made for communities to claim and install.

supportingSource.title: National Memorial for Peace and Justice — Wikipedia

assertion: Wrapped Reichstag — The artists used an immense skin of fabric to make the familiar Reichstag temporarily strange while leaving the building itself unchanged.
The Gates — The installation lined Central Park paths with 7,500 saffron-coloured vinyl frames and hanging fabric panels.

supportingSource.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Gates from the Roof

assertion: Rain Room — Random International’s work tracks movement and interrupts the downpour locally, creating a dry zone that follows each visitor.
Shibboleth — Salcedo used the fissure to address racial division, borders and the experience of immigrants; sealing it preserved a physical trace of the intervention.
the Parthenon Marbles — The surviving sculptures were split between Athens and London after Elgin’s agents removed roughly half of those then remaining at the Parthenon.
the Koh-i-Noor — The gem passed through several South and Central Asian rulers before reaching Queen Victoria; its ownership remains politically disputed.
the Benin Bronzes — The works once decorated the royal palace of the Kingdom of Benin; thousands entered European and American collections after the expedition.
the Euphronios Krater — Evidence linked the celebrated red-figure vase to an illegally excavated Etruscan tomb, leading to its transfer from the Met to Italy.
Victorious Youth — Also called the Getty Bronze, the statue’s find and export history underpin a continuing dispute over confiscation and ownership.
the Flatiron Building — Daniel Burnham’s steel-framed building fills the wedge where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue, producing its famous flat-iron plan.
the Dancing House — The stone tower represents Fred and the curving glass tower represents Ginger; together they form a dancing pair beside the Vltava.
the Centre Pompidou — Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers turned the building “inside out”; exposed services free the interior from many fixed obstructions.
Habitat 67 — Moshe Safdie developed the complex from his thesis, combining the density of apartments with light, air and outdoor space.
CCTV Headquarters — OMA’s design rejects a single vertical tower: its six linked sections form an irregular loop whose large cantilever meets high above the ground.
the Ecce Homo fresco in Borja — Cecilia Giménez attempted to restore Elías García Martínez’s deteriorating work in Borja; the altered image became popularly known as Monkey Christ.
Salvator Mundi — Restoration removed extensive later paint and repaired a split walnut panel; specialists continue to debate how much of the surviving work is Leonardo’s.
The Adoration of the Magi — Leonardo left the commission unfinished when he departed Florence; later cleaning stabilized the panel and made its complex preparatory work easier to read.
the Ghent Altarpiece — Conservation showed that much of the central Mystic Lamb’s face had been overpainted in the sixteenth century, hiding the original frontal gaze.
the Prado Mona Lisa — Infrared study found matching changes beneath both paintings, evidence that a pupil copied Leonardo’s work as it developed in the workshop.
the Cave of Altamira — María Sanz de Sautuola noticed the paintings while exploring with her father; experts initially rejected his claim that they were prehistoric.
the Riace bronzes — The two fifth-century-BC bronzes were found near Riace and are rare surviving examples of full-size ancient Greek bronze statuary.
Sanxingdui — A farmer uncovered jade relics in 1927; later excavations revealed a previously unknown Bronze Age culture with extraordinary bronzes.
the Lion-man — Fragments found in Germany’s Hohlenstein-Stadel cave form one of the oldest known zoomorphic sculptures in the world.
the Shigir Idol — The waterlogged peat preserved the carved larch figure; dating makes it the oldest known wooden sculpture.
Andy Goldsworthy — Goldsworthy works directly in landscapes with natural materials; melting, tides and decay are part of many works’ brief lives.
El Anatsui — Anatsui’s flexible metal sheets turn waste from the alcohol trade into works that can be folded and installed differently each time.
Louise Nevelson — Nevelson became known for monumental wall-like assemblages made from discarded wood and commonly painted black, white or gold.
Eva Hesse — Hesse’s experimental industrial materials gave her sculpture flexibility and translucency, but latex naturally yellows, cracks and becomes brittle.
Tara Donovan — Donovan discovers how one manufactured object behaves when repeated at architectural scale, transforming quantity into an apparently natural structure.
Milton Glaser — New York State recruited Glaser for the campaign in 1976; his taxi sketch developed into the stacked logo launched the following year.
Saul Bass — Bass transformed title sequences into concise visual overtures and also created enduring corporate marks for companies such as AT&T.
Paul Rand — Rand treated a logo as a simple, memorable sign; his IBM identity evolved into the familiar eight-bar version.
Otl Aicher — Aicher’s team used a strict grid, a light palette and standardized sports symbols intended to work across language barriers.
Jan Tschichold — Tschichold first codified modernist typography, then redesigned Penguin’s books through a consistent grid, spacing and typographic hierarchy.
the Coca-Cola contour bottle — Earl R. Dean’s 1915 design borrowed the ribbed curves of a cocoa pod after the team mistook it for a cola ingredient.
the Bic Cristal — Marcel Bich launched the inexpensive pen in 1950; its functional form entered design collections including New York’s Museum of Modern Art.
the Leica I — Barnack adapted cinema film for a larger still-image frame; the production camera succeeded after its 1925 Leipzig launch.
the Braun SK 4 — Rams joined Braun in 1955; the following year he and Gugelot designed the Phonosuper SK 4 known by this nickname.
the Juicy Salif — Alessi began producing the cast-aluminium object in 1990; its sculptural appearance made it a design icon despite criticism of its usefulness.
Times New Roman — The Times commissioned the face for newspaper setting; its compact proportions allowed many readable words to fit in a column.
Johnston — London Underground commissioned Johnston from Edward Johnston, making the typeface a foundation of the network’s visual identity.
Frutiger — Adrian Frutiger’s airport design was first called Roissy; it was expanded and released under his surname in 1976.
OCR-A — OCR-A was standardized for optical character recognition while remaining legible to human readers.
FE-Schrift — FE-Schrift was designed to hinder licence-plate forgery by making similar letters and digits visibly different.
the Rocky statue — A. Thomas Schomberg made the sculpture for Rocky III, and it later became a permanent Philadelphia attraction.
the Molly Malone statue — Jeanne Rynhart’s statue gives physical form to the heroine of the song commonly treated as Dublin’s unofficial anthem.
the Fremont Troll — Four local artists built the Fremont Troll beneath the Aurora Bridge in 1990, turning an awkward roadside space into a neighbourhood landmark.
Spoonbridge and Cherry — Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen designed the playful fountain sculpture for the Walker Art Center’s garden.
the Headington Shark — John Buckley made the rooftop shark for homeowner Bill Heine; planning disputes helped turn the work into a local symbol.
the Thomas Jefferson Building — Opened in 1897, the Beaux-Arts building was later named for the president whose book collection helped rebuild the Library of Congress.
the Long Room — It originally had a flat ceiling, shelves only on the lower level and an open gallery; in 1860 its roof was raised to accommodate an upper gallery.

assertion: Bibliotheca Alexandrina — Snøhetta’s circular design opened in 2002 as a contemporary library and cultural centre in Alexandria.
Seattle Central Library — The 2004 building reorganizes library functions into stacked platforms; its Books Spiral keeps nonfiction in one continuous numerical run.
Tianjin Binhai Library — MVRDV designed the auditorium sphere and flowing shelf-like terraces as the visual centre of the Binhai cultural district library.
Han van Meegeren — Van Meegeren confessed after the war and demonstrated his technique because selling a national treasure to Göring could have brought a treason charge.
Wolfgang Beltracchi — Beltracchi forged works in the styles of artists such as Max Ernst and created false provenance for the supposed Werner Jägers collection.
Elmyr de Hory — De Hory’s forged modernist drawings and paintings circulated through galleries, and his story became one of the film’s main threads.
John Myatt — Myatt painted imitations using modern household emulsion while Drewe manufactured provenance; police called it a major twentieth-century art fraud.
Shaun Greenhalgh — Greenhalgh worked with family members to create and sell objects attributed to many periods; the Amarna Princess was carved only weeks before its sale.
Tank Man — Several photographers captured the confrontation after the Tiananmen Square crackdown, making the unknown protester an international symbol.
Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima — Rosenthal photographed the second flag-raising on 23 February 1945; the image won a Pulitzer Prize and inspired a major memorial.

supportingSource.title: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima — Wikipedia

assertion: Dali Atomicus — Halsman used wires, assistants and repeated jumps rather than photomontage; the successful exposure took twenty-eight attempts.
The Horse in Motion — The 1878 photographs of Leland Stanford’s mare Sallie Gardner analysed motion in stages invisible to the unaided eye.
The Falling Man — Drew made a sequence of photographs as people fell from the World Trade Center; this frame became a difficult symbol of an individual death within the mass tragedy.
a mobile — Marcel Duchamp coined the term for Calder’s moving constructions, contrasting them with stationary sculptures called stabiles.
Tribute in Light — The public-art installation uses powerful searchlights near the World Trade Center site to evoke the former Twin Towers.
Kinetic Rain — Each droplet hangs from a motor-controlled cable, allowing the two-part installation to choreograph three-dimensional patterns.
Light-Space Modulator — The 1928–1930 kinetic work was first called Light Prop for an Electric Stage; the film A Lightplay: Black White Gray was based on it.
Homage to New York — Tinguely assembled it from found mechanical parts; timed sections activated in sequence until the planned self-destruction at the climax.
St Peter’s Basilica dome — Michelangelo simplified the earlier plans and strengthened the supporting piers; della Porta and Fontana completed the dome after his death.
the United States Capitol dome — The present Capitol dome was built during the nineteenth-century expansion and replaced a lower copper-covered wooden dome.
the Eden Project — The project reused a former clay pit; its lightweight hexagonal and pentagonal cushions create vast climate-controlled enclosures.
Gol Gumbaz — Completed for Sultan Mohammed Adil Shah, Gol Gumbaz is celebrated for its immense dome and strong acoustic echoes.
the Dome of Soltaniyeh — The fourteenth-century monument at Soltaniyeh is a major achievement of Ilkhanid architecture and one of the world’s largest brick domes.
Grand Central Terminal — The Main Concourse ceiling shows a Mediterranean winter sky; its reversed arrangement has been explained as a view from beyond the stars.
St Pancras railway station — William Henry Barlow engineered the single-span train shed, while George Gilbert Scott designed the Midland Grand Hotel façade.
São Bento railway station — Artist Jorge Colaço designed the vast tile panels installed in the station’s early-twentieth-century entrance hall.
Liège-Guillemins railway station — Built to accommodate high-speed trains, the station has nine tracks and five platforms.
Dunedin railway station — George Troup’s richly detailed station earned him the nickname “Gingerbread George”; the booking hall also has a mosaic floor.
the Unisphere — The Unisphere stands in Flushing Meadows–Corona Park on the former fair site and symbolizes global interdependence.
the Seattle Center Monorail — The short monorail opened before the fair and was retained as transit between Westlake Center and Seattle Center.
the Magic Fountain of Montjuïc — Carles Buïgas designed the large illuminated fountain as part of the exposition landscape on Montjuïc.
the Tower of the Sun — The tower rose through the roof of the fair’s Festival Plaza and was retained in Expo Commemoration Park after the event.
the Sunsphere — The Sunsphere was retained after the fair; its reflective panes were coloured with gold dust.
the Korean War Veterans Memorial — The nineteen figures and their reflections evoke the thirty-eight months of war and the 38th parallel.
the Oklahoma City National Memorial — The Field of Empty Chairs represents every person killed in the 1995 bombing, with smaller chairs for children.
the Diana, Princess of Wales Memorial Fountain — Kathryn Gustafson designed the low circular watercourse so visitors could approach and touch the flowing water.

supportingSource.title: Diana, Princess of Wales Memorial Fountain — Wikipedia

assertion: the Children’s Peace Monument — The monument honours Sadako and other children who died because of the atomic bombing; offerings of origami cranes became part of its commemorative tradition.
the Thiepval Memorial — The immense interlocking-arch monument commemorates those missing from the Somme battles between 1915 and 1918.
Cinderella Castle — The theme-park castle uses forced perspective: architectural elements shrink as they rise, exaggerating the apparent distance to the top.
Palazzo Spada — The forced-perspective gallery appears roughly four times its real length, ending with a small statue that looks life-size from the entrance.
Santa Maria presso San Satiro — Bramante compressed the apparent deep choir into about a metre of space using theatrical perspective.

supportingSource.title: Santa Maria presso San Satiro — Wikipedia

assertion: the Potemkin Stairs — The stairway’s changing width creates forced perspective; from the top only the landings are prominent, while from below the steps dominate.
the Mystery Spot — The attraction presents a gravity-hill illusion: a tilted environment distorts the visual cues people normally use to judge level and vertical.
